clinicalPearls: Uncommon sex cord-stromal neoplasm arising from Sertoli (nurse) cells; most occur in the testis and account for only a small fraction of testicular tumours, with rarer ovarian counterparts.
Typical presentation is a painless testicular mass or swelling; hormonally active tumours may cause gynaecomastia, reduced libido or, in children, endocrine effects.
The large majority are benign; malignant behaviour is suggested by large size, necrosis, high mitotic activity, marked cytological atypia, vascular invasion and extratesticular spread.
Recognised subtypes include Sertoli cell tumour NOS, large cell calcifying Sertoli cell tumour, sclerosing Sertoli cell tumour, and intratubular large cell hyalinising Sertoli cell neoplasia.
Large cell calcifying Sertoli cell tumour is frequently syndromic — bilateral, multifocal and calcified tumours arising in Carney complex (PRKAR1A) or Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (STK11/LKB1).
Intratubular large cell hyalinising Sertoli cell neoplasia is strongly linked to Peutz-Jeghers syndrome and may cause prepubertal gynaecomastia.

Serum germ-cell markers (alpha-fetoprotein and beta-hCG) are typically normal, and immunohistochemistry is positive for sex cord markers (inhibin, calretinin, steroidogenic factor-1, WT1) but negative for germ-cell markers (OCT3/4, SALL4, PLAP).
Management is testis-sparing or radical orchidectomy; malignant tumours respond poorly to chemotherapy and radiotherapy, and retroperitoneal nodal disease may need surgery.
reference.pathophysiology: Sertoli cell tumours are sex cord-stromal neoplasms derived from the Sertoli cell, the somatic supporting or nurse cell of the seminiferous tubule that normally sustains spermatogenesis and, through the sex cord lineage, shares an origin with the granulosa cell of the ovary. Many conventional (NOS) tumours carry activating CTNNB1 (beta-catenin) mutations with resulting nuclear beta-catenin accumulation and Wnt-pathway activation. The large cell calcifying subtype is characteristically associated with dysregulated cyclic-AMP / protein kinase A signalling through germline PRKAR1A mutation in Carney complex, and with germline STK11 (LKB1) mutation in Peutz-Jeghers syndrome; both may produce bilateral, multifocal, calcifying tumours. Because Sertoli cells can be steroidogenic, including aromatisation of androgens to oestrogen, some tumours are hormonally active and present with oestrogenic effects such as gynaecomastia.
additionalDifferentials: Leydig cell tumour and Sertoli-Leydig cell tumour (mixed sex cord-stromal tumours)
Granulosa cell tumour (adult and juvenile types)
Distinction among the Sertoli cell tumour subtypes themselves (NOS versus large cell calcifying versus sclerosing)
Seminoma and other germ cell tumours (clear-cell mimicry)
Testicular adrenal rest tumours (in congenital adrenal hyperplasia) and Leydig cell hyperplasia
Gonadoblastoma and unclassified sex cord-stromal tumour
additionalInvestigations: Scrotal ultrasound (hypoechoic mass; the large cell calcifying subtype shows characteristic calcification and may be bilateral or multifocal)
Serum germ-cell tumour markers (alpha-fetoprotein, beta-hCG, LDH), which are typically normal
Hormone profile where the tumour is hormonally active (oestrogens, testosterone, inhibin)
Histopathology with immunohistochemistry (inhibin, calretinin, steroidogenic factor-1, WT1, beta-catenin)
Staging cross-sectional imaging (CT chest, abdomen and pelvis) when malignant features are present
Genetic and syndrome evaluation for Carney complex (PRKAR1A) and Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (STK11) in large cell calcifying tumours
Echocardiography and screening for other Carney complex manifestations (cardiac myxoma, spotty pigmentation, endocrine tumours)
redFlags: Features suggesting malignancy: a rapidly enlarging or large tumour, necrosis or extratesticular extension
Manifestations of Carney complex (cardiac myxoma, spotty skin pigmentation, endocrine overactivity) with a calcifying testicular tumour
Mucocutaneous pigmentation and gastrointestinal polyps suggesting Peutz-Jeghers syndrome
Evidence of metastatic spread (retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy, pulmonary, hepatic or skeletal lesions)
reference.prognosis: Most Sertoli cell tumours are benign and cured by orchidectomy. Malignant variants carry a worse outlook because they metastasise to retroperitoneal nodes, lung, liver and bone and respond poorly to chemotherapy and radiotherapy, so complete surgical excision and staging are important.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosis as seminoma or another germ cell tumour when the cytoplasm is clear — resolved by the immunohistochemical marker profile.
Assuming all Sertoli cell tumours are benign and under-staging those with malignant features.
Missing the syndromic association of large cell calcifying tumours (Carney complex, Peutz-Jeghers), including bilateral disease.
Overlooking a small hormonally active tumour that presents with gynaecomastia before a mass is palpable.
Relying on normal serum tumour markers to exclude a testicular neoplasm.
management: Radical inguinal orchiectomy is the standard and usually curative treatment for Sertoli cell tumour, since most of these tumours are benign.
Testis-sparing excision may be considered instead of orchiectomy for a small, confidently benign mass, particularly when fertility or hormonal function preservation matters.

Adverse pathologic features on the specimen, vascular invasion, cellular atypia, necrosis, infiltrative margins, high mitotic rate, size over five centimetres, older age, high proliferation index, or aneuploidy, identify tumours at risk of metastasis and should prompt staging and closer follow-up.
When Sertoli cell tumours do metastasise, the retroperitoneal lymph nodes are the initial site of spread, so staging imaging should focus there first before extending to chest and distant sites.
No established chemotherapy or radiotherapy regimen is described for malignant Sertoli cell tumour; extrapolating a germ cell tumour regimen is not supported and should be avoided.

For nodal or oligometastatic malignant disease, surgical resection such as retroperitoneal lymph node dissection is the treatment with the clearest rationale, by analogy to the surgical-first approach used for related testicular sex cord tumours.

Hormonally active tumours can cause steroid hypersecretion and, in boys, precocious puberty; baseline and postoperative hormone assessment with monitoring for resolution of these features is reasonable.

Large cell calcifying and other syndromic subtypes are associated with Carney complex and Peutz-Jeghers syndrome and warrant genetic evaluation and family screening, especially if bilateral or multifocal.

For completely excised benign tumours, a period of clinical follow-up attentive to the surgical site and resolution of any hormonal symptoms is reasonable, with no specific surveillance schedule established.
Tumours with adverse histology or evidence of retroperitoneal or distant spread should be referred to a multidisciplinary genitourinary oncology team.
Suspected large cell calcifying subtype should be referred for genetics and syndrome evaluation given its association with Carney complex and Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.
